_note: GH#397 Phase 2 work order. register/tag are a reproducible heuristic proposal plus recorded hand-audit overrides (classification-overrides.json). Region lanes may re-judge any string, but must log the change.

strings.text: A coat over the chair back, good cloth, nobody in it. The table has two cups and one of them has been sitting there since before you arrived.
You set it down on a table nobody has claimed and it sits there being a package. Behind you a chair turns a quarter inch, so you pick it back up.
The coat is already over the chair back. You lay yours beside it, take the wrong one on the way past, and nobody in this room has raised a voice or an eye.
Two men at the far table are having a conversation you are not in. Tonight, that is all they are.
Two men at the far table who arrived together, ordered separately, and have been agreeing with each other about nothing for an hour.

strings.display_name: A Woman Who Came in a Carriage
strings.text: Gloves still on indoors, a chair chosen for its view of the door, and nothing at all on the table in front of her. She has been served and has not touched it.
He keeps the ledger of who is owed a table rather than who is owed money, which in this house is the more delicate book. He has not written anything down since you came in.

strings.display_name: A Gnoll with a Bad Ankle
strings.text: Boot off, ankle up on the bench, and a bowl of something going cold while she tells the story properly rather than quickly.
A full cup, untouched, at his right hand, and his chair turned three degrees off the table so he can see both doors without turning his head.
Built for a bigger room than this one, and kept fed accordingly. The chairs nearest it are the worst chairs in the house and they are always taken.
Bows, a cracked buckler, one very good spear. Nothing here was donated. Every piece was left behind by somebody who did not come back for it, and the house does not say which.
Elbow-polished to a shine along its whole length except one arm's width at the far end, which is somebody's, permanently.
Long enough for a full company and set for four. The house leaves it that way on purpose, and everybody in the room has noticed and nobody mentions it.
Names in three columns, and a fourth column with no heading. The fourth column is shorter than it was last season and nobody has rubbed it out.
Nine pegs. Eight have hats. The third from the left is empty and has been wiped, which is not the same as being unused.
You hang your hat on the third peg, brim out, the way the house does it. Across the room a man you have not looked at stops not looking at you.
A keg with a tapped face and an honest week's dents.
Its brother. Slightly fuller, slightly further from the door.
Coppers, a dog-eared deck, and chalk tallies in three different handwritings. The game never quite ends; it just changes players.
The wobbly one. Guests get it first.
The good stool. You'd have to earn it.
Banded oak, twice-locked, sitting where the quiet gentleman can count who looks at it.
Locked twice over. The quiet gentleman clears his throat, courteously.
Ledgers with no titles and boxes with no labels. Everything here is filed under later.
Army-neat. Whoever sleeps here folds corners like it still matters.
Less neat. A paperback under the pillow, spine broken at the same chapter.
Hats on pegs, every one accounted for. House rule says they stay on. Nobody explains the exceptions, and nobody asks twice.
Evening, {addr}. Fine weather for good behavior.
He inclines the hat half an inch — a genuine courtesy, not a performance of one. "A pleasure," he says, and seems to mean it.
A Gnoll in a vest cut sharper than his manners need to be, tall hat squared like it's holding a rank. He watches the room's exits before he watches you.

A slate by the cots, chalked in two hands: addresses with no names against them, times with no dates, and a column of initials down the edge. Small work. The Brothers keep the small work moving because the small work is how they hear things.
The slate is wiped clean. Come back when the chalk's been busy.
You take the top line off the slate and walk it across Invrisil: a package nobody described to you, to a door somebody did. Two gold, and the line is wiped before you're back through the alley.
Marker-holder's rate. The line you take is longer, the door further out, and nobody asks you to account for the way round you took getting there.
Even a couch here fits like it was fitted for you. The Brothers do nothing halfway, not even hospitality.
A person of discernment, Wilovan said. I withdraw one full half of my suspicions.
A short Drake in careful browns, floppy cap settled down over the neck-spines. His eyes did your full inventory the moment you stepped in, and he's too polite to say what it came to.
A broad man in a bowler hat, playing solitaire like the deck owes him money. Politely, though.
A Gnoll with a folded coat over one arm, keeping polite company with the hat stand and the door.
A Drake on a stool with his back to the wall, minding the shelf and the chest the way other men mind a fire.
A drink counter kept cleaner than the law would ever ask it to be.
Rings from a hundred glasses, sanded out and earned back.
Bottles arranged by loyalty rather than label. The top row is for after jobs that went well.
The Liscor stones were rougher. This one has been handled by people with better manners; it barely shows the wear.
A plain grey stone, out of place against the marble — until you notice the coin-gold vein running through it, and the frame of light waiting just under the surface.
Plum silk, a little too fine for the errand she's running. She counts her change twice.
Plum silk a season past its moment, worn on an errand that plainly sits beneath it. She counts the change twice and does not hide the second count.
A Gnoll traveler, tan road-cloak, watching the crowd the way a stranger watches weather.
A tan road-cloak with the dust still in the weave, and a Gnoll under it reading the crowd the way you would read weather coming.
Stacked shipping crates, waist-high, the kind of cover a man leans on to watch a street without looking like he's watching it.

You circle the block twice before it clicks: the modest COYLE AND SONS sign out front doesn't match the two wagons idling round the side, or the men counting crates like men who've been shorted before. Whatever Coyle's really running out of, the front door is the least of it.
A runner ducks out Coyle's side door with a ledger under one arm, moving with the particular haste of someone who'd rather not be noticed leaving.
You fall in a comfortable distance behind. The runner doesn't loop, doesn't double back — just walks like a man with somewhere specific to be, heading for the alleys off the boulevard's east end.
Nothing under the colonnade but shadow. Whoever works this corner keeps night hours only.
Two shapes peel off the shadowed colonnade, unhurried, the way people move when they've done this before. Only after dark.
A chalked ring on the cobbles, two of Coyle's regulars leaning against the wall beside it, already sizing you up.
Panes racked like coins on edge. The glazier watches the street through his own stock, which is either pride or advertising.
Boots on pegs, sorted by wear. The pair in the window has walked to Pallass and back, if the sign is honest. Signs here mostly are.
Three tables, steam on the glass, and a chalk line of prices that assumes you already know what smoke-leaf costs in Invrisil.

A modest hanging board, burgundy and brass, lettered COYLE AND SONS in a hand that cost more than the paint. The frontage behind it is one narrow door and a clean window. Everything that actually moves through this firm goes round the side, on wagons, after dark.
Slate roofs and chimney smoke. The city keeps its second story to itself.
[Eagle Eyes] — The rooftop line resolves into a second city: runners' shortcuts, a watcher over Coyle's block, and two gentlemen who are always politely elsewhere.
The rooftops run straighter than the streets. Somebody up there knows it.

Ruled paper in three weights, ink in four, and a card offering a scribe by the hour in a hand that is itself the advertisement. Half the contracts argued about on this street were bought here first, quietly, by both sides.

Every front on this stretch has stopped pretending to be busy. A wheel-track runs through the wet marble, wider than a trade wagon lays and far too clean, and it is already curving away three streets north.
Pink lacquer, gone before you turned your head. The boulevard takes a moment to remember it was doing something, and nobody on it says the name out loud.

A gap in the row of shopfronts, three strides wide and going darker the further in it goes. A stride past the wall line the paving changes underfoot, boulevard marble to whatever the alleys were laid with.
A house sign with no name on it, only a hand of cards face down and a hat on a peg. Half the silver in this city drinks here and none of it says so out loud.
Browsing, or selling?
He offers a smile with the price tag still visible on the underside. "Charming," he allows, in the tone of a man crossing an item off a ledger.
Coin-gold trim on a merchant's collar, rings enough to case a fist. He totals you before you've said a word — cheaply, by the look on his face.
A woman in a rose-dyed cloak checks a folded slip of paper against a shopfront number, unimpressed by both.
She holds the slip at arm's length, then the shopfront number, then the slip again. Whatever address she was given, this street declines to be it.
Blue-grey wool, city cut. She doesn't look at you. Nobody here looks at anybody.
Blue-grey wool, cut the way this city cuts it, and a walking pace she has no intention of breaking for you or anyone.
A porter's barrow, half-unloaded, and a man in no hurry to finish the other half.
The barrow is half empty and he is in no hurry about the other half. He has the arms for a faster day and has decided against one.
Olive work clothes, ink-stained cuffs. A clerk between one ledger and the next.
Olive work clothes, ink to the second knuckle, and a satchel worn flat on one side from the same walk every day.
Mustard-brown coat, city boots, the specific walk of a man pretending he isn't lost.
Mustard-brown coat, good city boots, and the specific unhurried circling of a man who will not be asking anybody.
The crate stack looks ordinary until you notice the angle: top-heavy, wedged to fall. Pulling from the bottom feels like a very bad idea.
You brace the stack and ease the wedge free by hand. Behind the bottom crate: a couple of coins someone forgot to collect.
Cleaned out — by you, earlier. The alley keeps its own inventory schedule.
A stack of crates wedged just wrong, top-heavy and set to come down on whoever pulls from the bottom. Old footpad mischief.
A back-alley apothecary's bench, crowded with someone else's half-finished work. None of it means anything to you.
Shelves of labelled jars, a rented burner, and a hand-lettered card: WORKING SPACE, BY THE HOUR, NO CREDIT.
[Low-Grade Synthesis] — Someone else's burner, your working. The draught comes out crude but honest, same as anywhere.
A cramped apothecary corner, its burner free for anyone who knows the working. Invrisil rents everything by the hour, including this.
A severe man at a spotless corner bench, tools laid out at right angles. Everything about him says the prices are exact and the opinions are free.

strings.display_name: A Back Door with a Ledger Behind It
strings.text: A back door with no handle on this side. Nothing about it is any of your business tonight.

strings.display_name: A Back Door with a Ledger Behind It
strings.text: A door with no handle on this side and a fresh scrape where somebody's boot goes when their hands are full. The ledger inside is worth more than the stock.

strings.display_name: A Back Door with a Ledger Behind It
strings.text: The Fence's strongbox gives up a lady's stone — forty years missing and still warm with someone else's guilt. It goes in your pack like it weighs more than it does.

strings.display_name: A Man with a Rented Table
strings.text: A folding table rented by the day, a cloth over it, and a brass block sitting on the cloth with two letters cut into the face. He has not covered it, because covering a thing is how a street learns you have one.
Two men paid by the week whether they work or not, and plainly out of practice.
You take the brass off the cloth yourself. Two letters, cut deep, and a table with nobody left standing beside it.
Tea's free. Rumor's a gold the cup.
She pours you a cup without being asked. "On the house," she says, "which is the only kind of trade I ever regret."
A tea-tray harness worn shiny at the left shoulder — she pours right-handed and listens left-eared. The cups are chipped. The ears are not.
Two figures loitering with the specific stillness of people about to stop pretending they're not waiting for you.
The second pair, closer to the counting-house door — same trick, same stillness, better light to see it by.
The desk's own ledger reads clean, which is exactly the kind of clean a man pays for. You don't have the eye to find the real one. Not yet.

The desk's own ledger reads clean — too clean, the kind of clean a man pays for. Whatever's real is hidden better than this. You'll want to know how this place is watched before you go digging further.

[Appraise Foe] — Now you know the gap in the watch, the true ledger comes easy: tucked behind a false-backed drawer no honest desk needs. Forty gold to a 'removal man,' dated the night before Coyle's own theft: his hand, his numbers, his mistake. The drawer's second catch gives up a shallow hidden safe behind it, empty now but scored where something heavier than coin sat until recently.
The clean ledger is the tell. Sizing up what is really here takes a practiced read.
Two men on the door, pacing something. You don't have the eye to time it yet.

[Appraise Foe] — Two men on the counting-house door, and they're sloppier than they think: the same slow circuit, the same gap while both backs are turned, near enough on the bell to set a watch by. Time it right and the desk inside is yours for a minute, maybe two.
Two men keep the counting-house door. Sizing up their rhythm takes a practiced read.
The runner's trail ends at a side door with fresh boot-scuff on the sill and burgundy-and-brass livery moving past the gap in the shutters. Coyle's crew, and no mistaking the building now.
The runner ducks inside, and you finally see the whole of it: crates stacked to the rafters, more of Coyle's livery than a legitimate warehouse ever needs. Wherever the come-along ends, it ends here.
Three men in burgundy-and-brass doublets, clubs and knives held like men who've used them before. Merchant-livery, not Watch steel — Coyle's, all the way down to the stitching.
A taut line crosses the alley at ankle height, tied off crate to drainpipe. It's clearly meant to trip someone. You can't see how to clear it safely.
You unhook the line and coil it loose. A couple of coins sit tucked in the crate it was tied to, payment nobody came back to collect.
The stash spot sits empty. Knowing this alley, someone will restock it.
A snag-line at ankle height, tied crate to drainpipe. Old footpad work, the kind meant to trip a running mark. Worth clearing.
Banked low, kept alive all day. Paper hates damp and this street sits in the river's breath every morning.

strings.display_name: A Lady with a Ring Box
strings.text: She has taken the chair furthest from the window and put a small hinged box on the table in front of her, closed. She has not opened it once in the time you have been standing here.
Cuffs pinned back, three nibs laid out in order of nerve, and the particular stillness of a man who is paid to have heard nothing.
Three weights, stacked lightest at the top, each with its price chalked on the edge of the shelf rather than the stock. Nothing here is priced where you can carry the number away.
Four inks, and the fourth is twice the price of the third for a difference you can only see in daylight. Somebody in this city has bought it every week for years.
Worn smooth in one narrow band where a hundred people a week have leaned to sign something they had already decided to sign.
A brass bell nobody rings, a blotter, and a small mirror angled so the man behind the counter can watch the door without appearing to.
Nine colours of wax and one blank seal for hire. The blank is the most used thing in the shop, by a distance.
Printed forms with the terms left open, sorted by how badly the second party will want to argue later. The thickest stack is the most reasonable-looking one.
A desk set at an angle that lets the scribe see the street and the street see nothing. There is a second chair, and it has been sat in recently.
